summary: Describes the format and syntax of a direction keyword used with bi-directional text in MIME, so mail can say whether text runs left to right or right to left.

plainLanguage.summary: Some languages read from right to left. This memo adds a label to messages saying which way to read.

subtitle: How to handle text that runs right-to-left (or switches direction) in email.

tldr.problem: Email standards assumed left-to-right text, but Hebrew and Arabic run right-to-left and can be mixed with English on the same line, requiring a way to specify directionality in MIME messages.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines character set suffixes (-i for implicit mode, -e for explicit mode) to indicate how bidirectional text should be interpreted, building on ECMA TR/53 standards for handling direction.
tldr.outcome: Mail systems can now correctly display mixed-direction text by including directionality keywords in the Content-type header (ISO-8859-6-i, ISO-8859-8-e, etc.), or defaulting to visual mode.

today: RFC 1556 standardized how MIME-based email handles bidirectional text. The visual mode remains the default and most widely supported. Implicit and explicit modes have seen limited adoption; modern systems more often use Unicode (UTF-8) with Unicode bidirectional algorithm support rather than these legacy character set extensions.

sections.title: The Problem of Bidirectional Text
sections.content: MIME standards (RFC 1521 and 1522) allowed any ISO language character set including Arabic (ISO-8859-6) and Hebrew (ISO-8859-8) to be transported in email. However, these languages are read right-to-left and can contain bidirectional data such as mixed Hebrew and English on the same line. Mail systems needed a way to specify the directionality so that display applications could render the text correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: English goes left to right, but Hebrew and Arabic go right to left. Email needs to say which way to read.

sections.title: Three Directionality Models
sections.content: The RFC defines three presentation methods: Visual directionality displays text according to only the primary (left-to-right) direction and is the simplest and default method for MIME. Implicit directionality determines direction by an algorithm based on character type and position (complex, detailed in ECMA TR/53). Explicit directionality uses control sequences interleaved within text to determine direction. The RFC provides examples for each: Content-type: text/plain; charset=ISO-8859-6-i for Arabic in implicit mode, or ISO-8859-8-e for Hebrew in explicit mode.
sections.plainLanguage: Visual mode is simplest: just show the text as-is. Implicit and explicit modes use algorithms or codes to say which way each part reads.

sections.title: Character Set Suffixes
sections.content: To specify directionality in MIME headers, the RFC extends character set names with suffixes: -i for implicit mode and -e for explicit mode. For example, ISO-8859-6-i indicates Arabic in implicit mode, while ISO-8859-8-e indicates Hebrew in explicit mode. When neither suffix is present, the default is visual mode. This scheme allows mail systems to know which algorithm or control-sequence method to apply when rendering the message body.
sections.plainLanguage: You add -i or -e to the character set name to say which way the text should be read.
